lines.text: Over seventy thousand kilometres of woven carbon, pulled tight between the Earth and an asteroid.
And every single metre of it ends right here, under your feet.
Welcome to New Angeles, the greatest city on Earth, and the only one with a ladder to the sky!
I'm Carmen, your NBN-certified guide, and this is Welcome to New Angeles, brought to you by the Space Elevator Authority.
Today we start at the very top, at the Root, and wander down the mountain to the port town that keeps it running.
Along the way I'll answer the question every visitor asks. Why on Earth would anyone build the greatest city in history on a volcano?
This is the Root, the anchor of the Beanstalk and the largest transit hub in the world.
It begins deep inside the mountain, at Earth Station Terminal, and climbs out of the rock until it rivals the starscrapers around it.
Inside you'll find five-star restaurants, boutiques, private homes, and kilometres of bright, safe corridors. Some visitors never go up at all. They just come to shop!
Trains leave from down below for Bogotá, Mexico City, and all the way to SanSan.
And there, rising straight out of the dome, is the tether itself. Twenty metres thick, dull grey, and perfectly, impossibly straight.
Up at four thousand seven hundred metres sits the Plaza del Cielo, the Plaza of the Sky.
It's sealed in clear transplas, because the air outside is thin and very cold. Inside it's buskers, sculpture gardens, and the best coffee stand in the hemisphere.
Do treat yourself to a hot YucaBean while you watch the beanpods rise. Somehow it tastes better at that altitude.
Locals swear that on a clear morning, from the overlooks, you can see all the way to the Amazon.
So, why here? A space elevator has to stand on the equator. That's orbital mechanics, and orbital mechanics does not negotiate.
And the equator runs almost exactly over the summit of Volcano Cayambe, one of the highest points on the equator anywhere on Earth.
Height means a shorter climb, solid rock means a firm grip, and a whole mountainside means room to grow.
There was a rival plan, you know. A floating base out in the Pacific. The Weyland Consortium explained, very publicly, why that was a terrible idea, and the rest is history.

And the volcano? It last erupted in seventeen eighty-six. Experts put the chance of a serious eruption at three thousandths of a percent per year, and the Root is protected by safety systems that would be material for its very own episode.
Now, the ride! Your beanpod is a cigar-shaped car, three decks high, gliding up the tether on mag-lev.
It speeds up for the first eighteen thousand kilometres, flips end over end, and brakes the rest of the way. Keep your seat restraints fastened for the flip.
About fifty minutes later you arrive at Midway Station, thirty-five thousand kilometres up, where everyone changes pods.
Beyond Midway waits the Castle, a five-kilometre asteroid towed into place to hold the whole thread taut.
And coming down the other way, every day, canisters of helium-three from the Moon. It fuels the fusion plants that power nearly the whole planet.
So the next time your lights come on, thank the Beanstalk.
Tired of the ground? The Space Elevator Authority invites you to ride the thread!
Fifty minutes to Midway. Zero pods lost. Snacks on every deck!
The Beanstalk. Going up!
Waiting list applies. Weyland Consortium royalties included in every fare. Passengers may be held in SEA Temporary Holding without notice. Yellow jackets are not responsible for motion sickness.
Building the Beanstalk took years of work and armies of builders, and the builders needed somewhere to live.
So the Consortium put up warehouses, dormitories and kitchens right here on the slope. That neighbourhood is called Eastside.
When the work was done, Chakana moved on to grander things. Eastside stayed, and its residents have shown remarkable creativity.
Look at the scaffolds and bridges strung between the towers. Locals cross the streets ten floors up, on walkways they built themselves.
And the colourful artwork on every wall comes from a local community group called the Polecats. Their signature is a polecat shaped like the Root.
Visitors are encouraged to enjoy Eastside from the plaza level.
Down the mountain we go, into Base de Cayambe, the Beanstalk's port town.
This is Old Town, where travellers sleep while they wait for their turn to go up-Stalk. Small hotels, clean beds, and signs in ten languages pointing to the Root.
The restaurants are family-run, and some families have cooked the same recipes since before the Beanstalk.
But now, let's ask a local about their story. Don Aurelio has run a hotel on this street for fifty years.
My father poured concrete for the Root. Twelve years of his life he dedicated to that thing.
One morning we woke up and this was not Ecuador anymore. Same house, same street, and yet we suddenly needed a permit to work in it.
But people still need a bed before they go up. So I make the beds.
Thank you, Don Aurelio! A living piece of history, everyone.
And that dome belongs to Old City Hall. In the early years, New Angeles was governed from right here.
Once the city grew up, the government moved south to Laguna Velasco. The clock tower stayed behind, and so did the pigeons.
My grandmother got married on those steps. She said the bells still remind her of that day.
Ha! Moving on.
Below the freight lines lies Mercado Baja, the Low Market. Kilometres of stalls under neon and holos, where the sun hardly ever reaches.
Anything that comes down the Beanstalk, and plenty that never went up it, ends up for sale here.
Bargaining is expected, cash is welcome, and questions are, shall we say, optional.
The locals have a saying here. See something, do nothing. It's very relaxing.
My tip? The noodles at the Luckier Lotus, on the edge of Mercado Baja. Oh, and if you ever find out what the broth's secret ingredient is that makes it so tasty, please tell me!
And here is the future! Neo-Broadway, the beating heart of Base de Cayambe, rebuilt by Watts-Watson Industrial Solutions.
When the Beanstalk was finished, Weyland sold its building machines, and Watts-Watson put them straight back to work.
Some towers are nearly finished. Others are paused for exciting reasons. The cranes work all night either way.
Time for "Speak like a local!"
Beanpod. The car that carries you up the Beanstalk. Never say "elevator car" here, people will know.
Up-Stalk and down-Stalk. Going to orbit, or coming home.
And plaza level. The bright, clean city of walkways and gardens, high above the streets. It's where all the most exciting things happen, and it's where the best New Angeles can be experienced.
Over half a billion people live in New Angeles today, in eleven districts on Earth and one on the Moon.
And every one of those districts grew, one way or another, from that grey thread on the mountain.
Next time we fly west to Rutherford and Akeidito, where the city finds out what happened today, and where to fly tomorrow.
Want the whole story of how the Beanstalk was built? Look for our special edition, The Weyland Years, wherever you get your NBN audio.
This was Carmen. Stay bright, stay safe, and stay on plaza level.
